tips.title: About Ijunta
tips.body:
Ijunta is a microlanguage which aims to be an aesthetically pleasing language to write, read, and speak.

It has a compact vocabulary and a flexible but simple system of affixes to express nuanced, socially robust meanings.

It is intended to be easy to pronounce by the majority of global speakers, using only common consonants and a simple 5 vowel system.

Learn more

tips.title: Syntax
tips.body:
Sentences and clauses in Ijunta are arranged in subject-verb-object (SVO) order.

Since most words may be flexibly used in multiple parts of speech, meaning must be inferred through position and context.

The word immediately following the subject noun phrase is always assumed to be a verb unless a subject complement is used as a copula.

The two primary complements are:

  • a - marks the next word / phrase as a noun complement, and
  • e - marks the next word / phrase as an adjective when following a noun, or as an adverb when following a verb.

For example:

  • Animale manja - The animal eats.
  • Animale a manja - The animal is food
  • A vasa - There is water
  • E vasa - It’s wet

The use of o marks the next word as the owner in an associative relationship with the preceding noun or attributional adjectives. For example:

  • Mi amo aroma o pan. - I like the smell of the bread.
  • Si uveni de seki o dia - He is coming tomorrow

When creating a question with interrogative pronouns, simply use the same sentence structure as a statement, but use the appropriate pronoun for the information being sought. For example:

  • Vendela e kaloke? - Where are the shops?.
  • Kato veni e kalite? - Who is coming tonight?

tips.title: Modifiers
tips.body:
Nouns
The following suffixes are used to systematically modify nouns:

  • -du, -edu: Make an abstract noun from adjective or verb; similar to English -ness, -ment
  • -la, -ela: Indicates a type of place or situation relating to the base noun
  • -le, -ale: Creates a group noun from a singular noun object
  • -ni, -i: Indicates an object of a type or kind, often diminutive, template for color names
  • -pi, -ipi: Indicates a person receiving an action or service
  • -ro, -ero: Marker of a person with a role or profession

The second form of suffix is used for words that end in m or n, or words that already end with that suffix (so not karoro, but karero for driver).

Verbs
Any verb can be intensified in its urgency, strength and/or power through addition of the suffix -ma. Use the suffix -mia/-nia instead if the word ends in m, ma, n, or na.

If an action as taking place in the past or future, prefix with du (past tense) or go (future tense).

The prefix me is used in situations where an action has not yet occurred, but is hypothesized as likely or possible. To actively push for the occurrence of the action or event, pair me with the -ma suffix to act as a command or demand; or -mia if already ending in -ma.

The prefix i- (or in- before vowels) is used in three situations:

  • To mark a verb as progressive tense – can also be paired with du or go)
  • To use as a gerund (noun form)
  • When paired with a verb of intent or causation such as deside (expect) or vole (want)

The prefix u- (or us- before vowels) is used to:

  • Indicate that an action is possible to complete, or that a state may occur in the future
  • Politely invite someone to undertake an action

When a u- prefix is combined with -ma, it acts as a polite request or exhortation; use -mia instead if the word already ends in -ma.

To make a verb passive, so the action describes something being done to the subject of the sentence, use the -re suffix. (Use the suffix -ure instead if the word ends in m, n, or re.)

tips.title: Connections & comparisons
tips.body:
Ijunta has a small range of flexible prepositions, with the most important being:

  • en: Being at a place or existing in a state (in, on, at [place], inside, on)
  • de: Origin, agent, or consideration of verb (from, of, about, by)
  • ada: A directed effort or targeting (to, at [time], into)
  • kon: A possession or co-location (with, among, during)

To reference relative distance of places, Ijunta uses a three-way distance contrast system with di (here), da (there) and vida (over there).

Ijunta conjunctions function mostly the same as in English, with the most important being:

  • an: and, also, furthermore
  • u: or, else, otherwise
  • pero: but, except, besides
  • ankora: yet, even still

Ijunta also has several idiomatic adverbial connecting phrases:

  • e junta: (consequential) so, as a result
  • e pende: (period of time) at the time that, when
  • e punto: (point in time) sometimes, from time to time, occasionally

These phrases can be combined with di or da to reflect a short-term or long-term focus, for example:

  • e da junta: eventually this means
  • e da pende: over the long term
  • e di punto: at this moment, right now
